title: The breaking of the vessels
hookLine: the vessels couldn't hold the light and shattered, scattering sparks

cards: Deep in Genesis there's a list that's easy to skim. "And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel." Then name after name.
And after every name but the last, the same short note: he died, and another reigned in his stead. Kabbalists slowed down at that list. Kings who rose and fell before anything could last.
To them it sounded like a hint of something at the very beginning: a first world that couldn't hold.

teach.b: Shevirat hakelim. The breaking of the vessels. It's the next scene in Luria's story, as Chaim Vital sets it down.
First, the vessels. After the line of light entered the open space, it needed containers: vessels to hold it and give it shape. Second, the breaking.
Some of the vessels could not hold it, and they shattered. Their pieces fell, and with them fell sparks of the light, scattered downward.
Kabbalists tied this to those kings of Edom: each one reigned, and each one died, a world that came and couldn't stay. Third, what's surprising.
In this picture, the breaking happens before there are any people at all. No one's mistake sets it off. It sits inside the story of the beginning itself.
Fourth, the sparks. The light didn't vanish when the vessels broke.
It's still there, down among the shards, mixed in with ordinary things. Everything else in Luria's teaching turns on that.
Some readers hear in it a word for a life: a marriage that came apart, a body that doesn't work the way it did, a plan that cracked down the middle.
In Luria's picture, broken pieces aren't empty. They're where the light landed. Today, it's enough to know the shards are carrying something.

how: The breaking of the vessels is studied in Lurianic Kabbalah through Chaim Vital's writings, and Jewish teachers often bring it up when speaking about loss and brokenness.

o: the tablets Moses smashed at the foot of the mountain
the glass broken under the canopy at a Jewish wedding
vessels that shattered under the light, scattering sparks

s: in Luria's story, the vessels break because people did wrong
the breaking comes before there are any people at all.
when the vessels broke, sparks of light fell with the pieces
the light was scattered, not lost.
in this teaching, the shards are empty
they hold the fallen sparks: everything else turns on that.

games.q: you are a vessel, made to hold the light. it pours in, stronger than you can hold. what does Luria's story say happens?
o: the vessel stretches and holds it all.
the vessel shatters, and sparks fall with the pieces.
the light turns back and leaves.
games.why: the vessels broke, and sparks of light fell with the shards, scattered below but not lost.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing in your life that's cracked: a chipped mug, a friendship that cooled, a habit you keep dropping, a part of your body that aches.
Don't try to fix it; let it be what it is, and then gently look for any light still in it, a memory, something it taught you, someone it brought closer.
If you find nothing, that's all right; simply rest beside it, without turning away.
